data.title: JPMorgan, BlackRock bid for slice of Singapore’s S$700 billion CPF
data.description:
JPMORGAN Asset Management, BlackRock and Endowus Singapore are the frontrunners to manage a slice of Singapore’s S$701 billion (US$543 billion) public pension fund.

The three firms submitted proposals to run a new investment programme that offers an alternative for members of the Central Provident Fund who want to earn more than the government-guaranteed return, according to people familiar with the matter.

The winners will be announced in the first half of 2027. Discussions are preliminary and no final decisions have been made, said the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private matters.

JPMorgan would partner with Singapore’s largest bank, DBS, in an extension of a retirement portfolio programme that was piloted in 2024. Endowus, an investment platform, is in talks to work with Capital Group on the CPF programme, said the people.

A spokesperson for the CPF Board said the evaluation process is ongoing, and it can’t comment on individual applications.

JPMorgan and Capital Group declined to comment. Endowus said it has been a digital adviser for investing CPF savings since 2019. BlackRock and DBS didn’t respond to requests for comment.

The investment plan was unveiled by Prime Minister Lawrence Wong in this year’s budget speech as a way to deal with the country’s aging population, and will be launched in 2028.

The new programme will allow members to opt in to portfolio strategies that automatically adjust according to their age. As investors get older, the equity allocation will shift to lower-risk assets such as bonds, before being liquidated in phases by a set target date.

Currently, members have the option of manually picking investments, including bonds, stocks and unit trusts, from a list of more than 30 asset managers. As of September, just S$22 billion – or 3 per cent – of net assets were invested in this optional plan, according to the CPF website.

The bulk of CPF savings are invested by the pension board in Special Singapore Government Securities. Proceeds from these securities are pooled with other government funds, including from budget surpluses and land sales, and managed by sovereign wealth fund GIC for long-term returns. Members under 55 earn risk-free interest of up to 5 per cent a year.

Founded in 1955, the CPF is Singapore’s mandatory pension fund for citizens and permanent residents to support retirement, housing and health-care needs. There are more than two million active members, and over S$14 billion in CPF contributions were received in the third quarter. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Stocks to watch: Kimly, AP Oil, Heptamax
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 26):

Kimly : The coffee shop operator reported a 30.8 per cent fall in net profit to S$12.8 million for its second half ended Sep 30, from S$18.5 million a year earlier. Revenue came in 1 per cent lower at S$161.1 million, from S$162.8 million previously. Kimly proposed a final dividend of S$0.01 a share for H2, bringing the total FY2026 dividend to S$0.02 a share. Shares of Kimly ended flat at S$0.365 on Wednesday, before the news.

AP Oil : The CEO of the petroleum products company, Ho Chee Hon, was sentenced to six months jail and a fine of S$25,000 for drink-driving on Wednesday. Accordingly, he will be away on a leave of absence for a period of six months from Dec 1. The company said that the charges are personal in nature and unrelated to its business or operations. Its board added that Ho remains suitable to continue in his role as CEO. Shares of AP Oil ended flat at S$0.126 on Wednesday, before the update.

Heptamax : The industrial solutions company, which is proposing to buy a data centre company for S$500 million in a reverse takeover, has been queried by the Singapore Exchange Regulation over the deal. Among other things, the regulator asked how the valuation for the target company Racks Central was arrived at. It also asked Heptamax to give details of the beneficial owners of the vendor. The company replied that the price was arrived at on a willing-buyer, willing-seller basis, taking into account Racks Central’s earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation for FY2025, among other things. Heptamax ended flat at S$0.131 on Wednesday.

data.title: Philippine trade deficit hits record as imports soar 50% in October
data.description:
THE PHILIPPINES posted a record trade deficit in October as a 50 per cent surge in imports outpaced another sharp rise in exports.

October’s trade deficit was US$6.95 billion, preliminary data from the Philippine Statistics Authority showed on Friday (Nov 27). That is the widest since 1980 and 65.6 per cent more than a year earlier, based on Bloomberg data.

Imports rose to a record-high US$17.52 billion, as electronics products soared 147.4 per cent and telecoms equipment surged 65.7 per cent.

Imports of mineral fuels and cereals also showed significant increases for the South-east Asian nation that relies heavily on imported oil and rice.

The imports jump outpaced another record-breaking month for exports, which rose 41.8 per cent to US$10.6 billion.

The artificial intelligence boom boosted demand for semiconductors and devices such as personal computers and smartphones.

The Philippine central bank forecasts a current account deficit of US$19.1 billion for 2026, before widening further to US$19.4 billion in 2027.

The peso was at 63.71 against the US dollar, flat from its close on Thursday. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Japan, Hong Kong banks set to improve in 2027 while Australia deteriorates: Fitch
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Banking conditions across the Asia-Pacific (Apac) are set to remain broadly sound in 2027, though a divergence is emerging among the region’s developed markets, according to Fitch Ratings.

In its banking outlook reports for developed and emerging markets released on Thursday (Nov 26), the credit rating agency assigned “improving” outlooks to the banking sectors in Japan and Hong Kong, while downgrading Australia’s to “deteriorating”.

Meanwhile, the banking sector outlook across the region’s emerging markets was kept “neutral”, with the Philippines the sole market to receive an “improving” call.

“Fitch Ratings expects broadly stable operating conditions for most Apac developed-market banking systems in 2027, with higher interest rates supporting net interest margins (NIMs) and earnings in most markets,” the agency said in its developed markets report.

In Japan, continued interest-rate normalisation is a key tailwind for the country’s major banks. Fitch forecasts the country’s policy rate to reach 2 per cent by end-2027.

“Higher domestic interest rates and continued asset repricing are likely to strengthen earnings generation and internal capital formation, while a more active business environment provides additional revenue opportunities,” Fitch noted.

“Sustained inflation, wage growth and solid corporate activity should continue to support lending demand, transaction activity and fee-generating businesses,” the report added.

Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s banking sector, which entered 2026 on a “deteriorating” outlook before being revised to “neutral” in the first half of the year, was also upgraded to “improving” for 2027.

“Easing commercial real-estate market pressures – alongside solid wealth-management income and cross-border activity – underpin Hong Kong’s improvement,” Fitch said.

The agency expects Hong Kong banks’ core profitability to improve in 2027, as pressure on margins and asset quality recedes, while wealth-related fee-income growth remains solid.

“We expect credit costs to decline further over 2027, reflecting early signs of property-market stabilisation and the provisioning that banks have already built in prior years.”

Australia diverges

In contrast, Australia stands out as the sole developed market moving to a “deteriorating” outlook, from “neutral”.

“We expect a combination of higher-for-longer interest rates and a weakening labour market to weigh on asset quality, while strong competition and high investment requirements are likely to constrain earnings growth,” Fitch said.

Loan growth is also likely to slow, constrained by higher interest rates and decelerating economic growth.

Still, the agency offered reassurance on the sector’s buffers. “Losses should remain manageable, given a decade of conservative underwriting, a heavy weighting towards residential mortgages and strong collateral positions,” it said.

Singapore holds steady

Closer to home, Singapore banks remain on a “neutral” outlook.

“We expect Singapore banks to deliver another year of strong performance in 2027, building on robust results in 2026, while global uncertainty remains a downside risk,” Fitch said.

A higher Singapore Overnight Rate Average is likely to support NIMs, while sustained wealth-management inflows should drive mid to high single-digit growth in fee and commission income.

“Strong provision coverage and conservative underwriting standards leave banks well-positioned to absorb stresses should any emerge,” the agency added.

Emerging markets cushioned

Across emerging Asia-Pacific markets, eight of nine banking systems are on “neutral” outlooks.

Fitch said it expects financial performance for most Apac emerging market banking systems in 2027 to be broadly in line with 2026.

The Philippines is the lone emerging market with an “improving” banking sector, rebounding from weak economic growth and elevated consumer impairments in 2026.

“Accelerated public investments in infrastructure projects should drive economic growth and corporate loan demand in 2027,” Fitch said. It projected the Philippines’ loan growth to pick up to 11 per cent from 10 per cent, while credit costs decline to 1 per cent from 1.3 per cent.

China and Thailand both carry “neutral” outlooks for 2027 after entering 2026 on “deteriorating”.

For China’s banking sector, where system loan growth is projected at 5 to 6 per cent, Fitch said: “We expect NIMs to improve marginally, as a flat policy rate and lower deposit costs from repricing should more than offset pressure on loan yields.”

Thai banks are likewise set for steady performance as they gradually work through legacy bad debt.

Meanwhile, India and Indonesia remain among the region’s strongest growth markets, with double-digit loan expansion forecast at around 15 per cent for India in FY2028 and 10 per cent for Indonesia in 2027, although higher credit costs will limit profitability upside.

Looking ahead, Fitch flagged persistent inflation, tighter-for-longer monetary conditions, renewed geopolitical tensions and weaker global growth as key downside risks for Apac’s banking sector.

“Softer artificial intelligence-related demand or geopolitical shocks would pressure growth and asset quality, with South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore most exposed,” the agency warned.

Nevertheless, resilient asset quality, generally adequate capital buffers and broadly stable profitability leave Apac banks well-positioned to weather these headwinds, Fitch said.

data.title: Stocks to watch: Jardine Matheson Holdings, Hongkong Land, Marco Polo Marine
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Nov 27):

Jardine Matheson Holdings (JMH) , Hongkong Land : JMH announced on Thursday that Adam Keswick – whose family controls the Jardine group – will step down from the board effective Dec 31, 2026. He will also step down from the board of Hongkong Land. JMH ended Thursday at US$60.38, up US$0.25 or 0.4 per cent, while Hongkong Land was US$0.07 or 0.8 per cent higher at US$8.53, before the announcement.

Marco Polo Marine : The marine logistics company posted on Friday a 56 per cent drop in net profit to S$21.3 million for its second half ended Sep 30, 2026, from S$47.9 million in the previous corresponding period. Revenue for H2 rose 11 per cent to S$78 million from S$70.1 million. Earnings per share stood at S$0.0055 for the half-year period, down from S$0.0128. Shares of Marco Polo Marine ended at S$0.093 on Thursday, S$0.005 or 5.7 per cent higher.

data.title: Why a professional baseline for HR is a reasonable expectation
data.description:
IF THE pace of change feels faster, it is because it is. New artificial intelligence systems are arriving at speed and organisations are moving them from experiments into everyday workflows.

In conversations with business and human resources (HR) leaders, I hear the same questions: Which tasks should be automated? How should decisions be made? And how must operating models evolve to ensure that technology improves performance without leaving people behind?

For workers, these are not abstract questions. Familiar tasks may disappear while new ones emerge. Skills built over many years may no longer be enough.

The result is a mixture of anticipation and anxiety, particularly when change affects a person’s livelihood, career prospects and sense of what lies ahead.

Technology is only one part of this transformation. Singapore is also facing rapid population ageing.

In 2026, citizens aged 65 and above made up 21.4 per cent of Singapore’s citizen population, placing the country above the threshold commonly used to define a super-aged society.

As more people remain in the workforce for longer, employers will need to redesign jobs, provide flexible work arrangements and build workplaces where different generations can contribute and learn from one another.

The regulatory landscape is also evolving. Parliament has passed the Workplace Fairness Act and the accompanying dispute-resolution legislation, both of which are scheduled to take effect at the end of 2027.

Employers will need stronger systems for fair employment decisions, grievance handling and documentation. What was once guided mainly by tripartite norms will increasingly carry statutory obligations and consequences.

Taken together, these shifts raise a straightforward question: What should employers and workers be able to expect from the professionals who advise on decisions that carry legal risk and can alter working lives?

This question lies at the heart of the recent report by the Tripartite Workgroup on Human Capital Capability Development, which sets out five recommendations to strengthen Singapore’s human capital capabilities.

One proposal has attracted particular attention: from Jul 1, 2028, organisations with more than 200 employees will need at least one HR professional certified at the Institute for Human Resource Practitioners (IHRP) Certified Professional level or higher.

Recognised equivalent accreditations may also qualify, subject to applicable bridging requirements.

These concerns are understandable. A certificate cannot capture everything that makes a good HR professional. It cannot fully measure empathy, courage or judgment, nor predict how someone will respond when an employee’s role is at risk or a business faces a painful restructuring.

Neither should experienced practitioners without certification be dismissed as incapable; many have built deep expertise over decades.

However, the limits of certification are not an argument against a professional baseline.

When someone advises on employment rights, workplace fairness, grievances or restructuring, employers and workers should have confidence that the individual has demonstrated a recognised foundation of HR knowledge, ethics and professional judgment.

A baseline should also not be mistaken for a one-off examination that divides the capable from the incapable. Professional certification should be a continuing commitment: a standard that evolves with business, technology, regulation and workforce expectations.

IHRP’s framework is anchored in its Body of Competencies, which was first introduced in 2016 and subsequently refreshed in 2020 and 2024 through engagement with business and HR leaders, tripartite partners and the wider ecosystem.

Some have pointed out that experience matters more. Indeed, experience remains indispensable. It deepens perspective and helps practitioners recognise patterns that no textbook can teach.

Yet, experience can also harden into familiar assumptions. Pairing it with an evolving professional standard gives practitioners reason to test what they think they know, update their knowledge and keep their judgment current.

There is a broader point here about the standing of HR I hope can be further debated. When people think of the professions on which society depends, they often cite medicine, law, accountancy and engineering.

HR should be part of this conversation too. HR practitioners apply specialised knowledge, exercise professional judgment, uphold ethical standards and advise on decisions with serious consequences for individuals and organisations.

Professional recognition should reflect this level of responsibility. This requirement is an important step towards positioning HR alongside other recognised professions – a profession that our community can be proud of.

IHRP, for its part, has work to do. Certification must remain rigorous, accessible and relevant. The standards must keep pace with generative AI, flexible work, new workforce models and the responsible use of people data.

Recertification must reflect genuine professional development rather than become a passive pay-to-maintain exercise. Together with learning and ecosystem partners, we must give practitioners practical ways to learn, find mentors, exchange experience and support one another.

Ultimately, the measure of professionalisation will not be the number of certificates issued. It will be whether employment practices become fairer, workforce planning improves, difficult decisions are handled more responsibly and trust in HR grows.

A professional baseline cannot guarantee these outcomes. However, at a time when employers face increasingly complex and consequential decisions, it is a reasonable place to start.

The writer is chief executive officer of the IHRP

data.title: China’s Cabinet stresses market support in rare statement; vows more moves to stabilise stocks
data.description:
CHINA’S State Council reaffirmed its support for the capital market in a rare midday readout of its meeting, emphasising the role of the so-called national team and pledging to roll out more policies to stabilise equities.

Beijing will improve policies guiding long-term funds into stocks and encourage listed companies to step up dividend payouts and share buybacks, according to the Xinhua News Agency. 

The statement comes at a precarious time for Chinese stocks, with most equity benchmarks entrenched in a bear market amid tepid earnings and a weak economy.

The CSI 300 Index has lost 16 per cent so far in 2026, putting it on track for its worst year since 2022.

While authorities sought to revive investor confidence through a slew of measures in October and state funds have been actively buying, they have mostly been seen as stemming the bleeding rather than engineering a recovery. 

“The statement shows that stabilising the capital market remains a priority at the highest levels of government, which should help ease negative sentiment,” said Fu Zhifeng, chief investment officer at Shanghai Chengzhou Investment Management.

“After the recent sell-off, investors have shown little appetite to buy the dip, while much of the selling pressure may have already been exhausted. The announcement can therefore provide further support to the market this afternoon.” BLOOMBERG

data.title: Asean must counter economic nationalism with deeper integration, wider partnerships: DPM Gan
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Asean must counter rising economic nationalism with deeper integration and wider partnerships, in a world where governments are placing more emphasis on self-reliance and control over critical industries, said Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong on Nov 27.

“Raising barriers among ourselves would narrow the opportunities available to each of us,” he said. A more integrated Asean would strengthen its value as a partner, while broader tie-ups open up more opportunities for the region.

Gan, who is also Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade), was delivering a keynote speech at SPH Media’s Asia Future Summit 2026, jointly presented by The Straits Times, The Business Times, Lianhe Zaobao, Berita Harian and Tamil Murasu.

The annual event gathered policymakers, business leaders and industry experts, with OCBC as the presenting sponsor, Marina Bay Sands as the official venue partner and Amazon Web Services as the official cloud partner.

In his speech, Gan identified three factors that make integration and partnerships especially important: artificial intelligence, geopolitical shocks and geo-economic contestation. “Each can strengthen the impulse to turn inward. Yet each also makes cooperation more crucial,” he said.

His remarks followed the United States’ announcements of fresh tariffs and chip export restrictions over the past two weeks, moves which affected many in South-east Asia as the region finds itself in the crosshairs of sharpening rivalry between Washington and Beijing.

“Geo-economic competition is reshaping the networks through which we trade, invest and access technology,” Gan said, with governments paying closer attention to dependencies and control over critical capabilities.

“Asean countries cannot determine how major powers manage their differences,” he added. “But we can maintain relationships across these divides and remain a bridge for trade, investment and cooperation.”

Doing so would require that Asean earn and sustain its partners’ confidence in the grouping’s integrity, institutional reliability and business environment by issuing clear and predictable rules, upholding its laws and commitments, and taking firm action against wrongdoing, he said.

“As scrutiny of international trade and investment intensifies, maintaining these standards becomes even more important,” he added.

ASEAN will mark its 60th anniversary in 2027, with Singapore pushing for deeper integration and wider partnerships as it takes on Asean’s rotating chairmanship at a time of heightened geopolitical contestation.

Both the US and China would continue to be key economic partners for Asean, Gan said, with their businesses, technologies and markets important to the region’s growth.

Both countries are among the region’s largest trading partners and sources of foreign direct investment.

In tandem, the grouping is strengthening tie-ups with other partners that would expand the region’s economic options and reduce its exposure to disruptions, Gan said.

These include negotiations to upgrade Asean’s trade agreements with South Korea and Canada, moves to expand and enhance the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, and growing links with other regional groupings such as the European Union and Gulf Cooperation Council.

Asean is also strengthening integration within the grouping, with Gan highlighting recent efforts that would help firms better tap suppliers and customers within the region.

A recently upgraded Asean Trade in Goods Agreement, set to be rolled out in end-2026, will help businesses reduce costs through streamlined procedures and more transparent rules, he said, while a customs-related mutual recognition arrangement would give trusted traders faster clearances and priority treatment in participating countries.

And a regional Digital Economy Framework Agreement signed earlier in the month would make cross-border transactions, payments and access to digital services easier, he added.

These would make Asean more valuable as a place to produce and market to serve, and form a stronger regional base enabling the grouping to “engage the world with greater confidence”, Gan said. THE STRAITS TIMES
